name: Aldabra Atoll
blurb: Giant tortoises, coconut crabs and frigatebirds on a remote coral atoll.

tip.title: Remove the tortoises
tip.text: About 100,000 giant tortoises graze the turf and scrub. Lower their numbers and watch the tortoise turf, land crabs, coconut crabs and the flightless rail respond.

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Aldabra, Aldabra giant tortoise, Coconut crab). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Microscopic algae in the lagoon and the surrounding sea. They feed corals, flying fish and the rest of the open-water web.

nodes.name: Green turtle
nodes.desc: Nests on Aldabra in large numbers. Adults graze seagrass and algae in the shallow lagoon.

nodes.name: Hawksbill turtle
nodes.desc: Lives on reefs and eats sponges, corals and other invertebrates. Breeds on the atoll.
Fast predator of the reefs and lagoon edges, hunting other fish.
Top predator of the surrounding sea. It takes turtles of all sizes as well as fish.
Tropical sun drives growth in the lagoon, on the reef and on land.
Fresh water is scarce, and tortoises take most of their moisture from their food. Rain sets how well the turf and scrub grow.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and small invertebrates that break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil.

story: Aldabra, in the Outer Islands of the Seychelles, is the world's second-largest coral atoll, 1,120 km southwest of Victoria. It has no surface freshwater. Arab seafarers named it for its harsh, sun-baked environment.
matters: It is home to the Aldabra giant tortoise, one of the largest tortoises in the world. Many other Indian Ocean giant tortoises were driven to extinction by European sailors.
